title: Thebans
capsule: By the mid-fourth century BCE Thebes, leader of the Boeotian Confederacy, had lost the brief hegemony it won at Leuctra and was drained by the long Third Sacred War (356–346) against Phocis over control of Delphi—a struggle in which Thebes invited Philip II of Macedon into central Greece, bringing Macedonian power to its doorstep. Alarm at Philip's advance led Thebes to abandon its Macedonian alignment and, persuaded by the Athenian orator Demosthenes, to join Athens in a last coalition to block him. At Chaeronea in 338 BCE the allied army was crushed and the Theban Sacred Band annihilated to a man; Philip stripped Thebes of its dominion over Boeotia and installed a Macedonian garrison on the Cadmea, ending Theban independence in this era.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Theban military and political power in 371–362 BCE is exceptionally well documented in Xenophon, Diodorus Siculus, and Plutarch; the 'territorial' extent at any moment reflects narrative sphere of influence rather than fixed boundaries.
